text.tspan: A model that writes one token at a time can still be trained on every token of a sentence at once. This page shows the trick, and what it costs.

text.style: fill:var(--ink);font-family:'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;font-size:14px;font-weight:600

text.tspan: called teacher forcing. It hands the decoder the CORRECT previous tokens, all at once, and asks every position to predict the token that comes next, all in parallel. There is one danger: if
, it could simply copy the answer. The causal mask from
shift and the mask are two halves of one idea — neither works without the other.

tspan.style: font-family:'DejaVu Sans Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'Courier New', monospace;font-size:12.4px;font-weight:600;fill:var(--ink)

text.tspan: real weakness of this scheme: during training the model never sees its own mistakes.

, add x back, normalise — the first of three in a decoder
layer. What comes out is "the output so far, in context": each position now carries information from every earlier
position. This is exactly what cross-attention will use as its queries when it goes looking in the source sentence.

Training and generation, set side by side

Teacher forcing is how the model is trained, not how it is used. The difference between the two columns below is a real weakness of this training scheme, not a detail of the code: the model never practises recovering from its own mistakes.
